Cell death overview

Cell death

  • Stress on cell => growth adaptations
  • Severe stress on cell => cell injury => cell death

Morphologic hallmark of cell death

  • Loss of nucleus via
  • Pyknosis
  • Karyorrhexis
  • Karyolysis

Mechanisms of cell death

  • Necrosis
  • Apoptosis

Necrosis

  • Death of a large group of cells followed by acute inflammation
  • Due to underlying pathologic process; never physiologic
  • It is the major pathway of cell death in many commonly encountered injuries
  • Divided into several types based on gross features
  • Coagulative necrosis
  • Liquefactive necrosis
  • Gangrenous necrosis
  • Fat necrosis
  • Fibrinoid necrosis

Coagulative necrosis

  • Cell shape and organ structure are preserved because the injury denatures structural proteins and enzymes limiting proteolysis of dead tissue for days to weeks after injury
  • Necrotic tissue that remains firm
  • Nucleus disappears

Coagulative necrosis

  • Dead tissue is digested by lysosomal enzymes of recruited leukocytes and cellular debris is removed by phagocytosis after several days to weeks
  • Characteristic of ischemic infarction of any organ except brain

Coagulative necrosis

  • Area of infarcted tissue is often wedge-shaped and pale

Red infarction

  • It occurs if blood re enters a loosely organized tissue
  • Example: red infarction of the testicle

Liquefactive necrosis

  • Necrotic tissue that becomes liquefied
  • Enzymatic digestion of cells and proteins results in liquefaction

Occurs in

  • Brain infarction
  • Abscess
  • Pancreatitis

Gangrenous necrosis

  • A term that refers to coagulative necrosis of a limb (generally lower leg) and GI tract when blood supply has been lost
  • It is on two types: dry gangrene, but if superimposed infection occurs then liquefactive necrosis occurs (wet gangrene)

Caseous necrosis

  • Necrotic tissue appears as friable yellow-white (cheese like)
  • Combination of coagulative and liquefactive necrosis
  • Occurs in granulomatous inflammation due to TB or fungal infection

Fat necrosis

  • Focal areas of necrotic adipose tissue
  • Appears as chalky white lesions due to released fatty acids combining with calcium

Fat necrosis

  • Occur in
  • Trauma to fat (e.g. breast)
  • Pancreatic mediated damage of peripancreatic fat

Saponification

  • Fatty acids released by trauma or lipase join with calcium
  • Example of dystrophic calcification

Fibrinoid necrosis

  • Necrotic damage to blood vessel wall
  • Leaking of proteins into vessel wall results in bright pink staining
  • Characteristic of malignant hypertension or vasculitis

Apoptosis

  • Energy-dependent, genetically programmed cell death
  • Involves single cells or small groups of cells
  • Examples
  • Endometrial shedding during menstrual cycle
  • Removal of cells during embryogenesis
  • CD8+ T cell- mediated killing of virally infected cells

Apoptosis Morphology

  • Dying cell shrinks (becomes eosinophilic)
  • Nucleus condenses and fragments
  • Apoptotic bodies fall from cell and are removed by macrophages; not followed by inflammation

Apoptosis is mediated by caspases

  • Activate proteases (break down cytoskeleton)
  • Activate endonucleases (break down DNA)

Caspases are activated by multiple pathways

  • Intrinsic mitochondrial pathway
  • Extrinsic receptor-ligand pathway
  • Cytotoxic CD8+ T cell pathway

Intrinsic mitochondrial pathway

  • Cellular injury, DNA damage, or decreased hormonal stimulation inactivates Bcl2
  • Cytochrome c leaks from inner mitochondrial matrix into cytoplasm

Extrinsic receptor-ligand pathway

  • FAS ligand binds FAS death receptor (CD 95) on target cell
  • TNF binds TNF receptor on target cell

Cytotoxic CD8+ T cell pathway

  • Perforins create pores in membrane of target cell
  • Granzyme enters pores and activates caspases
Necrosis Apoptosis
Cell size Enlarged (swelling) Reduced (shrinkage)
Nucleus Pyknosis => karyorrhexis => karyolysis Fragmentation into nucleosome sized fragments
Plasma membrane Disrupted Intact; altered structure
cellular contents Enzymatic digestion Intact
Inflammation Yes No
Physiologic vs pathologic Always pathologic Often physiologic

Other mechanisms of cell death

  • Necroptosis
  • Pyroptosis
  • Ferroptosis

Autophagy

  • Lysosomal digestion of cell’s own components
  • It is a survival mechanism in times of nutrient deprivation that enables the cell to live by eating its own components
  • Involves the formation of autophagic vacuole
